content.text:
The child who says "Why am I like this?"

Too slow at running, too short, not as good as their friends — as children grow, they naturally begin to compare themselves to others. And one day, shoulders slumping, they sigh, "I'm nothing special."

In moments like these, a single word from a parent can shift the direction of a child's heart. And the warmest tool for lifting a child out of the swamp of comparison is a story.

Curious about the plot of this self-esteem story? Explore the lesson of the self-esteem story alongside its illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the story, too. Read the self-esteem story together with your child and talk it over. From toddler self-esteem to self-esteem building stories and stories about individuality, we've gathered many ways to enjoy 23. Hori Is Hori!

content.alt: 23. Hori Is Hori! - Why should self-esteem take root early?
content.text:
Why should self-esteem take root early?

Self-esteem isn't about 'being better than others' — it's the feeling of 'liking myself just as I am.' When this feeling settles firmly in early childhood, a child doesn't crumble easily in the face of failure.

On the other hand, a child who grows up always comparing themselves to others loses sight of even their own strengths. That's why, in the early years, it matters more than anything to repeat the message: "You are special because you are you."

content.alt: 23. Hori Is Hori! - What Mom asked Hori
content.text:
What Mom asked Hori

In the story Hori Is Hori!, Hori resents his short, only-colorful tail. That's when Mom sits him on her lap and asks, "When Toto draws a picture, which colors does he use?"

"So what about Hori's tail?" With Mom's question, Hori realizes something: his rainbow-colored tail can fill the whole sky with color. Toto is Toto because he's fast, Bori is Bori because he's big, and — "Hori is Hori!"

Discovering your own special sparkle on Tangobook

The heart of this story is the message: it's okay to be different from others — your own color is your own special sparkle. A child naturally feels that what makes each of us different is what makes each of us charming.

Tangobook stories repeat "Hori is Hori!" like a refrain, helping children joyfully remember the message of self-respect. The scene where color pops back into the tail that had drooped gray stays in a child's heart for a long time.

content.alt: 23. Hori Is Hori! - Finding your child's strengths together at home
content.text:
Finding your child's strengths together at home

After reading the book, look for your child's own strengths together. Smiling easily, being great at helping friends, having a wonderful imagination — it doesn't have to be a visible skill. Give it a name: "This is what makes you special."

And put your child's name in and chant it together: "○○ is ○○!" When you share words of individuality often instead of words of comparison, your child learns to love themselves just as they are.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How can I build my child's self-esteem?

A. Rather than comparing your child to others, acknowledge them just as they are and express your love. Celebrate small challenges and achievements together so the feeling of "I'm good because I'm me" can grow.

Q. How does a self-esteem story help my child?

A. By watching the main character treasure themselves, your child learns to cherish themselves too. Self-esteem stories warmly plant the strength to grow up being your true self.

Q. What should I say when my child lacks confidence?

A. Notice the effort and the process rather than the result, and tell them they are enough just as they are. When you hug them and say it's okay to make mistakes, they find the courage to try again.
